claim: Loss of the pulmonary lineage specifier NKX2-1 augments the growth of KRAS-driven lung adenocarcinoma.
source: Loss of the pulmonary lineage specifier NKX2-1 augments the growth of KRAS-driven lung adenocarcinoma and causes pulmonary to gastric transdifferentiation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known finding from previous work.

claim: Loss of NKX2-1 causes pulmonary to gastric transdifferentiation in KRAS-driven lung adenocarcinoma.
source: Loss of the pulmonary lineage specifier NKX2-1 augments the growth of KRAS-driven lung adenocarcinoma and causes pulmonary to gastric transdifferentiation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known finding from previous work.

claim: FoxA1 and FoxA2 are required for initiation of mucinous NKX2-1-negative lung adenocarcinomas in the mouse.
source: Here, we show that the transcription factors FoxA1 and FoxA2 are required for initiation of mucinous NKX2-1-negative lung adenocarcinomas in the mouse and for activation of their gastric differentiation program.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figures 1-2.

claim: FoxA1 and FoxA2 are required for activation of the gastric differentiation program in mucinous NKX2-1-negative lung adenocarcinomas.
source: Here, we show that the transcription factors FoxA1 and FoxA2 are required for initiation of mucinous NKX2-1-negative lung adenocarcinomas in the mouse and for activation of their gastric differentiation program.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figures 1 and 3.

claim: Foxa1/2 deletion severely impairs tumor initiation in NKX2-1-negative lung adenocarcinomas.
source: Foxa1/2 deletion severely impairs tumor initiation and causes a proximal shift in cellular identity, yielding tumors expressing markers of the squamocolumnar junction of the gastrointestinal tract.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by tumor burden data in Figure 2A.

claim: Foxa1/2 deletion causes a proximal shift in cellular identity, yielding tumors expressing markers of the squamocolumnar junction of the gastrointestinal tract.
source: Foxa1/2 deletion severely impairs tumor initiation and causes a proximal shift in cellular identity, yielding tumors expressing markers of the squamocolumnar junction of the gastrointestinal tract.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by single-cell RNA-seq and IHC data in Figure 3.

claim: FoxA1/2 expression is downregulated in the squamous component of murine lung adenosquamous carcinoma.
source: In contrast, we observe downregulation of FoxA1/2 expression in the squamous component of both murine and human lung adenosquamous carcinoma.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by IHC data in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: FoxA1/2 expression is downregulated in the squamous component of human lung adenosquamous carcinoma.
source: In contrast, we observe downregulation of FoxA1/2 expression in the squamous component of both murine and human lung adenosquamous carcinoma.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by IHC data in Figure 4D-E.

claim: FoxA1/2 loss in established KRAS-driven neoplasia originating from SPC-positive alveolar cells induces keratinizing squamous cell carcinomas.
source: Using sequential in vivo recombination, we find that FoxA1/2 loss in established KRAS-driven neoplasia originating from SPC-positive alveolar cells induces keratinizing squamous cell carcinomas.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figures 5-6.

claim: NKX2-1, FoxA1 and FoxA2 coordinately regulate the growth and identity of lung cancer in a context-specific manner.
source: Thus, NKX2-1, FoxA1 and FoxA2 coordinately regulate the growth and identity of lung cancer in a context-specific manner.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract, synthesizing findings from all experiments.

claim: Absence of NKX2-1 in lung adenocarcinoma correlates with non-pulmonary cellular identities and poor prognosis compared with NKX2-1-positive tumors.
source: In lung adenocarcinoma, absence of the pulmonary lineage specifier NKX2-1/TTF1 correlates with non-pulmonary cellular identities and poor prognosis compared with NKX2-1-positive tumors (Barletta et al., 2009; Cardnell et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to prior literature.

claim: Loss of NKX2-1 is sufficient to cause lineage switching in a mouse model of KRASG12D-driven lung adenocarcinoma.
source: In previous work, we and others have shown that loss of NKX2-1 is sufficient to cause lineage switching in a mouse model of KRASG12D-driven lung adenocarcinoma (Maeda et al., 2011; Snyder et al., 2013; Tata et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to prior work.

claim: Nkx2-1 deletion in established tumors causes cancer cells to shed their pulmonary identity and adopt a gastric-like differentiation state.
source: Nkx2-1 deletion in established tumors causes cancer cells to shed their pulmonary identity and adopt a gastric-like differentiation state characterized by extensive mucin production and expression of multiple gastrointestinal markers, including HNF4α and Gastrokine 1.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to prior work.

claim: NKX2-1-deficient tumors morphologically resemble invasive mucinous adenocarcinoma (IMA).
source: These tumors morphologically resemble a subtype of human lung cancer called invasive mucinous adenocarcinoma (IMA), which also expresses gastrointestinal markers and is predominantly driven by KRAS mutations (Guo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to prior literature.

claim: Invasive mucinous adenocarcinoma expresses gastrointestinal markers and is predominantly driven by KRAS mutations.
source: These tumors morphologically resemble a subtype of human lung cancer called invasive mucinous adenocarcinoma (IMA), which also expresses gastrointestinal markers and is predominantly driven by KRAS mutations (Guo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to prior literature.

claim: Approximately 10–15% of human lung adenocarcinomas express HNF4α with no detectable NKX2-1.
source: Approximately 10–15% of human lung adenocarcinomas express HNF4α with no detectable NKX2-1 (9), including both IMAs and more moderately differentiated tumors.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to prior work.

claim: In many NKX2-1-negative tumors, the NKX2-1 gene appears to be silenced by genetic and/or epigenetic mechanisms.
source: In many of these tumors, the NKX2-1 gene appears to be silenced by genetic and/or epigenetic mechanisms (Hwang et al., 2016; Matsubara et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to prior literature.

claim: The Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 (PRC2) appears to play a role in suppressing mucinous differentiation in KRAS-driven, p53-deficient lung adenocarcinoma.
source: Aside from NKX2-1 itself, the Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 (PRC2) appears to play a role in suppressing mucinous differentiation in KRAS-driven, p53-deficient lung adenocarcinoma (Serresi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to prior literature.

claim: Many gastrointestinal transcripts expressed in IMA are known targets of FoxA1 and FoxA2.
source: Many of the gastrointestinal transcripts expressed in IMA are known targets of the forkhead box transcription factors FoxA1 and FoxA2 (FoxA1/2).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction, drawing on established knowledge of FoxA1/2 target genes.

claim: FoxA1 and FoxA2 govern the development of a variety of tissues and are expressed in both the adult lung and GI tract.
source: These transcription factors govern the development of a variety of tissues and are expressed in both the adult lung and GI tract (reviewed in Golson and Kaestner, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to a review article.

claim: FoxA1/2 are expressed in both murine and human IMA.
source: FoxA1/2 are also expressed in both murine and human IMA (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by IHC images in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: Nkx2-1 deletion in autochthonous lung tumors caused FoxA1/2 to re-localize from the regulatory elements of pulmonary-specific genes to those of genes expressed in both the GI tract and IMA.
source: We previously found that Nkx2-1 deletion in autochthonous lung tumors caused FoxA1/2 to re-localize from the regulatory elements of pulmonary-specific genes (such as Sftpa1) to those of genes (such as Hnf4a) that are expressed in both the GI tract and IMA (Snyder et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to prior work.

claim: NKX2-1 physically interacts with FoxA1/2.
source: Given that NKX2-1 physically interacts with FoxA1/2 (Snyder et al., 2013; Minoo et al., 2007), we hypothesized that NKX2-1 promotes FoxA1/2 interaction with regulatory elements of the pulmonary differentiation program at the expense of those governing gastric identity.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to prior literature.

claim: Tumors lacking either FoxA1 or FoxA2 are indistinguishable from control tumors by morphology and immunohistochemistry.
source: Initial evaluation by morphology (H and E) and immunohistochemistry (IHC) showed that tumors lacking either FoxA1 or FoxA2 were indistinguishable from control tumors (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by images in Figure 1A.

claim: Concomitant deletion of Foxa1 and Foxa2 led to the emergence of small neoplastic lesions devoid of glandular architecture and mucin production.
source: In sharp contrast, concomitant deletion of Foxa1 and Foxa2 led to the emergence of small neoplastic lesions (Figure 1A, right column) in the alveoli that were completely devoid of the glandular architecture and mucin production that characterizes NKX2-1-deficient tumors.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by images in Figure 1A.

claim: Absence of mucin production in Foxa1/2-deficient lesions was demonstrated by Alcian Blue staining and IHC for Muc5AC.
source: Absence of mucin production was apparent by H and E staining and further demonstrated by Alcian Blue staining (Figure 1B) and IHC for Muc5AC (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by images in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Cytokeratin 8 (CK8) was expressed in lesions arising in mice of all genotypes.
source: Cytokeratin 8 (CK8) was expressed in lesions arising in mice of all genotypes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), showing that cells lacking all three transcription factors retained an epithelial identity and did not undergo a complete epithelial to mesenchymal transition.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by IHC images in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Cells lacking NKX2-1, FoxA1 and FoxA2 retained an epithelial identity and did not undergo a complete epithelial to mesenchymal transition.
source: Cytokeratin 8 (CK8) was expressed in lesions arising in mice of all genotypes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), showing that cells lacking all three transcription factors retained an epithelial identity and did not undergo a complete epithelial to mesenchymal transition.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and inferred from CK8 expression data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: HNF4α and PDX1 are transcription factors that regulate gastrointestinal differentiation and are expressed in human invasive mucinous adenocarcinoma.
source: HNF4α and PDX1 are transcription factors that regulate gastrointestinal differentiation and are expressed in human invasive mucinous adenocarcinoma and mouse models of this disease (Snyder et al., 2013; Skoulidis et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to prior literature.

claim: HNF4α, PDX1, and PK-L were undetectable in FoxA1/2-deficient neoplasia.
source: Both transcription factors, as well as the HNF4α target PK-L, were undetectable in FoxA1/2-deficient neoplasia (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by IHC images in Figure 1C.

claim: Gastrokine 1, Cathepsin E and Galectin 4 were not expressed in FoxA1/2-deficient lesions.
source: Additional markers of gastrointestinal differentiation, including Gastrokine 1, Cathepsin E and Galectin 4, were also not expressed in these lesions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by IHC images in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Gastrointestinal markers were retained in lesions lacking either FoxA1 or FoxA2 alone.
source: All these markers were retained in lesions lacking either FoxA1 or FoxA2 alone (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by IHC images in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: FoxA1 and FoxA2 are required for mucin production in NKX2-1-negative lung tumors in a functionally redundant manner.
source: Taken together, these data show that FoxA1 and FoxA2 are required for mucin production and key elements of the gastrointestinal differentiation program in NKX2-1-negative lung tumors in a functionally redundant manner.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section, synthesizing data from Figure 1.

claim: FoxA1 and FoxA2 are required for key elements of the gastrointestinal differentiation program in NKX2-1-negative lung tumors in a functionally redundant manner.
source: Taken together, these data show that FoxA1 and FoxA2 are required for mucin production and key elements of the gastrointestinal differentiation program in NKX2-1-negative lung tumors in a functionally redundant manner.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section, synthesizing data from Figure 1.

claim: Most lesions in KrasLSL-G12D/+; Nkx2-1F/F; Foxa1F/F; Foxa2F/F mice exhibited complete loss of FoxA1/2 expression when analyzed at 11 weeks post-infection.
source: Most lesions in KrasLSL-G12D/+; Nkx2-1F/F; Foxa1F/F; Foxa2F/F mice exhibited complete loss of FoxA1/2 expression when analyzed at 11 weeks post-infection.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: KrasLSL-G12D/+; Nkx2-1F/F; Foxa1F/F; Foxa2F/F mice harbored a variable but substantial quantity of tumors that retained FoxA1 or FoxA2 as well as targets such as HNF4α.
source: However, these mice also harbored a variable but substantial quantity of tumors ('incomplete recombinants') that retained FoxA1 or FoxA2 as well as targets such as HNF4α (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: Incomplete recombinants were often larger than complete recombinants at 11 weeks post-infection.
source: Since incomplete recombinants were often larger than the lesions lacking NKX2-1, FoxA1 and FoxA2 (i.e. 'complete recombinants') (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), we speculated that they might have gradually outgrown the complete recombinants over time.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by images in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: At 5 weeks after tumor initiation, incomplete recombinants comprised a much smaller proportion of overall tumor burden than at 11 weeks.
source: Consistent with this possibility, we found that 5 weeks after tumor initiation, incomplete recombinants comprised a much smaller proportion of overall tumor burden than at 11 weeks (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: Concomitant deletion of both Foxa1 and Foxa2 led to an approximately 10-fold reduction in tumor burden when measured at 5 weeks post-initiation.
source: We found that concomitant deletion of both Foxa1 and Foxa2 led to an approximately 10-fold reduction in tumor burden when measured at 5 weeks post-initiation (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by quantitative data in Figure 2A.

claim: Deletion of either Foxa1 or Foxa2 alone had little to no effect on tumor burden at 5 weeks post-initiation.
source: In contrast, deletion of either Foxa1 or Foxa2 alone had little to no effect on tumor burden.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2A.

claim: BrdU incorporation was reduced by ~50% in FoxA1/2-deficient lesions in comparison with control lesions.
source: BrdU incorporation was reduced by ~50% in FoxA1/2-deficient lesions in comparison with control lesions (Figure 2B–C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by quantitative data and images in Figure 2B–C.

claim: FoxA1/2-deficient lesions proliferate at a significantly lower rate than controls as measured by MCM2 and KI67.
source: IHC for the proliferation markers MCM2 and KI67 also demonstrated that FoxA1/2-deficient lesions proliferate at a significantly lower rate than controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E–G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by quantitative data and images in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E–G.

claim: The apoptotic rate of FoxA1/2-deficient lesions was no different than controls as measured by IHC for cleaved caspase-3.
source: In contrast, the apoptotic rate of FoxA1/2-deficient lesions was no different than controls as measured by IHC for cleaved caspase-3 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by IHC images in Figure 2—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Deletion of both Foxa1 and Foxa2 led to a dramatic increase in survival (median survival 293 days) compared to controls (median survival 143–160 days).
source: Mice in the three control groups survived for a similar duration after tumor initiation (median survival 143–160 days). In contrast, deletion of both Foxa1 and Foxa2 led to a dramatic increase in survival (median survival 293 days).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by survival curve data in Figure 2D.

claim: Approximately 80% of the tumor burden in KrasLSL-G12D/+; Nkx2-1F/F; Foxa1F/F; Foxa2F/F mice consisted of mucinous HNF4α-positive adenocarcinomas in survival analysis.
source: Histopathologic analysis showed that approximately 80% of the tumor burden in KrasLSL-G12D/+; Nkx2-1F/F; Foxa1F/F; Foxa2F/F mice consisted of mucinous HNF4α-positive adenocarcinomas (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by quantitative data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Extensive extracellular mucin secretion was observed in the tumors of KrasLSL-G12D/+; Nkx2-1F/F; Foxa1F/F mice.
source: We also noted extensive extracellular mucin secretion in the tumors of KrasLSL-G12D/+; Nkx2-1F/F; Foxa1F/F mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by H&E images in Figure 2—figure supplement 1I.

claim: Lack of FoxA1/2 activity at tumor initiation severely impairs the proliferation and long-term growth potential of NKX2-1-negative lung adenocarcinoma.
source: Taken together, these data show that lack of FoxA1/2 activity at tumor initiation severely impairs the proliferation and long-term growth potential of NKX2-1-negative lung adenocarcinoma.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section, synthesizing data from Figure 2.

claim: A total of 134 cells were considered to be of sufficient quality for single-cell RNA-seq analysis.
source: A total of 134 cells were considered to be of sufficient quality for further analysis (Supplementary files 1–2), which yielded three distinct clusters (tSNE plot, Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the tSNE plot in Figure 3A.

claim: Single-cell RNA-seq analysis yielded three distinct clusters.
source: A total of 134 cells were considered to be of sufficient quality for further analysis (Supplementary files 1–2), which yielded three distinct clusters (tSNE plot, Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the tSNE plot in Figure 3A.

claim: Cluster 1 (C1) contained cells from mice of all three genotypes.
source: Cluster 1 (C1, n = 62 cells) contained cells from mice of all three genotypes.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the single-cell RNA-seq analysis.

claim: Cluster 1 marker genes included canonical NKX2-1 target genes Sftpa1 and Sftpb.
source: These included canonical NKX2-1 target genes Sftpa1 and Sftpb (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the single-cell RNA-seq analysis.

claim: Cluster 1 represents tumor cells that are phenotypically NKX2-1-positive.
source: From these data, we infer that C1 represents tumor cells that are phenotypically NKX2-1-positive.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the marker gene data.

claim: Cluster 2 (C2) only contained cells from KrasLSL-G12D/+; Nkx2-1F/F and KrasLSL-G12D/+; Nkx2-1F/F; Foxa1F/F; Foxa2F/F mice.
source: In contrast, cluster 2 (C2, n = 31 cells) only contained cells from KrasLSL-G12D/+; Nkx2-1F/F and KrasLSL-G12D/+; Nkx2-1F/F; Foxa1F/F; Foxa2F/F mice.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the single-cell RNA-seq analysis.

claim: Numerous gastrointestinal transcripts were identified as marker genes for cluster 2, including Hnf4a, Gkn1, Lgals4 and Ctse.
source: Numerous gastrointestinal transcripts were identified as marker genes for this cluster, including Hnf4a, Gkn1, Lgals4 and Ctse.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the single-cell RNA-seq analysis.

claim: Cluster 2 appears to include incomplete recombinants from KrasLSL-G12D/+; Nkx2-1F/F; Foxa1F/F; Foxa2F/F mice that express sufficient levels of FoxA1 and/or FoxA2 to maintain a gastric differentiation state.
source: Thus, C2 appears to include incomplete recombinants from KrasLSL-G12D/+; Nkx2-1F/F; Foxa1F/F; Foxa2F/F mice that express sufficient levels of FoxA1 and/or FoxA2 to maintain a gastric differentiation state.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the marker gene data.

claim: Cluster 3 (C3) contained only cells from KrasLSL-G12D/+; Nkx2-1F/F; Foxa1F/F; Foxa2F/F mice.
source: In contrast, cluster 3 (C3, n = 41 cells) contained only cells from KrasLSL-G12D/+; Nkx2-1F/F; Foxa1F/F; Foxa2F/F mice and expressed marker genes not characteristic of either a pulmonary or gastric differentiation state, suggesting that C3 likely contains cells completely deficient for NKX2-1, FoxA1 and FoxA2 (i.e. complete recombinants).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the single-cell RNA-seq analysis.

claim: Cluster 3 expressed marker genes not characteristic of either a pulmonary or gastric differentiation state.
source: In contrast, cluster 3 (C3, n = 41 cells) contained only cells from KrasLSL-G12D/+; Nkx2-1F/F; Foxa1F/F; Foxa2F/F mice and expressed marker genes not characteristic of either a pulmonary or gastric differentiation state, suggesting that C3 likely contains cells completely deficient for NKX2-1, FoxA1 and FoxA2 (i.e. complete recombinants).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the single-cell RNA-seq analysis.

claim: Cluster 3 likely contains cells completely deficient for NKX2-1, FoxA1 and FoxA2 (complete recombinants).
source: In contrast, cluster 3 (C3, n = 41 cells) contained only cells from KrasLSL-G12D/+; Nkx2-1F/F; Foxa1F/F; Foxa2F/F mice and expressed marker genes not characteristic of either a pulmonary or gastric differentiation state, suggesting that C3 likely contains cells completely deficient for NKX2-1, FoxA1 and FoxA2 (i.e. complete recombinants).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the marker gene data.

claim: There is a strong correlation (Pearson correlation coefficient = 0.62) between differentially expressed genes identified in single cell and bulk RNA-seq analyses.
source: We then performed RNA-Seq on sorted bulk tumor cells from KrasLSL-G12D/+ and KrasLSL-G12D/+; Nkx2-1F/F mice (n = 3 each, Supplementary file 4) and found a strong correlation (Pearson correlation coefficient = 0.62) between the differentially expressed genes identified in single cell and bulk analyses (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by correlation plot in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Normal murine type two pneumocytes clustered with presumptive NKX2-1-positive C1 cells.
source: We also compared our single-cell datasets with published data from other groups. We found that normal murine type two pneumocytes (Treutlein et al., 2014), which are the presumed cell of origin for NKX2-1-positive tumor cells, clustered with presumptive NKX2-1-positive C1 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by tSNE plot in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The IMA signature caused C2 cells to cluster separately from other cells in PCA analysis.
source: We also used principal component analysis (PCA) to compare our single-cell data with a gene signature of human IMA (Guo et al., 2017). In this analysis, the IMA signature caused C2 cells to cluster separately from the other cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by PCA plot in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: C2 cells are more similar to IMA than C1 and C3.
source: This shows that C2 cells are more similar to IMA than C1 and C3, as would be expected if they represent the NKX2-1-negative tumor cell population.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the PCA analysis.

claim: In tSNE analysis, C1 was most similar to normal lung.
source: In both approaches, we found that C1 was most similar to normal lung, and that C2 was most similar to glandular stomach.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by tSNE plot in Figure 3B.

claim: In tSNE analysis, C2 was most similar to glandular stomach.
source: In both approaches, we found that C1 was most similar to normal lung, and that C2 was most similar to glandular stomach.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by tSNE plot in Figure 3B.

claim: C3 cells clustered near the upper GI tract, in particular the forestomach and esophagus.
source: C3 cells clustered near the upper GI tract, in particular the forestomach and esophagus.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by tSNE plot in Figure 3B and HCPC plot in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: C3 cells are not as closely related to esophagus/forestomach as C1 and C2 are to lung and glandular stomach, respectively.
source: However, cosine similarity analysis (Supplementary file 6) showed that C3 cells are not as closely related to esophagus/forestomach as C1 and C2 are to lung and glandular stomach, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by cosine similarity data in Supplementary file 6.

claim: The vast majority of complete recombinants cells do not express ΔNp63 or cytokeratin 5 (CK5).
source: Moreover, the vast majority of complete recombinants cells do not express ΔNp63, a master regulator of squamous differentiation, or the squamous marker cytokeratin 5 (CK5) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by IHC images in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Complete ablation of NKX2-1, FoxA1 and FoxA2 causes lung tumor cells to adopt an identity that is neither pulmonary nor gastric, but also is not fully squamous.
source: Thus, complete ablation of NKX2-1, FoxA1 and FoxA2 causes lung tumor cells to adopt an identity that is neither pulmonary nor gastric, but also is not fully squamous.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section, synthesizing data from Figure 3.

claim: A small but discrete transitional zone exists at the squamocolumnar junction (SCJ) of the gastrointestinal tract, just proximal to the glandular stomach.
source: Recent studies have described a small but discrete transitional zone at the squamocolumnar junction (SCJ) of the gastrointestinal (GI) tract, just proximal to the glandular stomach, which is not included as a discrete entity in our tissue panel.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to prior literature.

claim: The transitional zone at the SCJ consists of a bilayered epithelium expressing high levels of cytokeratin 7 (CK7).
source: This transitional zone consists of a bilayered epithelium expressing high levels of cytokeratin 7 (CK7) (Jiang et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2011), including a ΔNp63/CK5-positive basal layer and a ΔNp63/CK5-negative luminal layer.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to prior literature.

claim: Complete recombinants in KrasLSL-G12D/+; Nkx2-1F/F; Foxa1F/F; Foxa2F/F mice have uniformly high levels of CK7 protein that are comparable to the SCJ.
source: Intriguingly, complete recombinants in KrasLSL-G12D/+; Nkx2-1F/F; Foxa1F/F; Foxa2F/F mice have uniformly high levels of CK7 protein that are comparable to the SCJ (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by IHC images in Figure 3C.

claim: Several genes specifically expressed in C3 vs. both C1 and C2 are expressed at high levels at the SCJ of the GI tract and/or the cervix, including Chil4, Gda, Mmp7, and Vcam1.
source: Manual inspection of genes specifically expressed in C3 vs. both C1 and C2 (using both SC3 and SCDE) revealed that several of these genes are expressed at high levels at the SCJ of the GI tract and/or the cervix. These genes include Chil4 (Nio et al., 2004), Gda and Mmp7 (Herfs et al., 2012), and Vcam1 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to prior literature and supported by IHC images in Figure 3C.

claim: Other C3-specific genes are expressed at higher levels throughout the forestomach and esophagus than glandular stomach, including Cav1, Cdh13, Hilpda, Fbln2 and Rbp7.
source: Other C3-specific genes are expressed at higher levels throughout the forestomach and esophagus than glandular stomach, including Cav1, Cdh13, Hilpda, Fbln2 and Rbp7 (Uhlén et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation to prior literature.

claim: Protein levels of several C3-specific genes are much higher in complete recombinants than in NKX2-1-negative lesions.
source: Using IHC, we found that protein levels of several these genes are much higher in complete recombinants than in NKX2-1-negative lesions (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by IHC images in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: FoxA2 expression ends at the SCJ and is absent throughout the squamous forestomach and esophagus.
source: Interestingly, FoxA2 expression ends at the SCJ and is absent throughout the squamous forestomach and esophagus.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by IHC images in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: FoxA1 levels are very low but detectable at the SCJ then increase in the proximal forestomach and esophagus.
source: In contrast, FoxA1 levels are very low but detectable at the SCJ then increase in the proximal forestomach and esophagus.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by IHC images in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Overall FoxA1/2 levels appear to reach their nadir at the SCJ and distal forestomach of the normal murine GI tract.
source: Thus, overall FoxA1/2 levels appear to reach their nadir at the SCJ and distal forestomach of the normal murine GI tract.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from IHC data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: FoxA1/2 are required for NKX2-1-deficient lung tumor cells to adopt a gastric identity.
source: Taken together, our data show that FoxA1/2 are required for NKX2-1-deficient lung tumor cells to adopt a gastric identity.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section, synthesizing data from Figures 1-3.

claim: Concomitant loss of NKX2-1 and FoxA1/2 at tumor initiation leads to a distinct differentiation state characterized by expression of multiple markers of the transitional epithelium normally found at the SCJ of the GI tract.
source: Moreover, concomitant loss of NKX2-1 and FoxA1/2 activity at tumor initiation leads to a distinct differentiation state characterized by expression of multiple markers of the transitional epithelium normally found at the SCJ of the GI tract.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section, synthesizing data from Figure 3.

claim: A subset of KrasLSL-G12D/+; Nkx2-1F/F; Foxa1F/F and KrasLSL-G12D/+; Nkx2-1F/F; Foxa2F/F mice developed macroscopic adenosquamous carcinomas (AdSCCs) at 20 weeks post-initiation.
source: Although KrasLSL-G12D/+; Nkx2-1F/F; Foxa1F/F and KrasLSL-G12D/+; Nkx2-1F/F; Foxa2F/F mice exhibited minimal obvious phenotypes at early timepoints (Figures 1–2), we found that a subset of these mice developed macroscopic adenosquamous carcinomas (AdSCCs) at 20 weeks post-initiation (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: No AdSCCs were found in any of the KrasLSL-G12D/+; Nkx2-1F/F mice aged to 20 weeks post-initiation.
source: In contrast, we did not find AdSCCs in any of the KrasLSL-G12D/+; Nkx2-1F/F mice aged to 20 weeks post-initiation.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: Human AdSCC is an uncommon but aggressive lung cancer subtype that contains a mix of clonally related adenocarcinoma and squamous cell components.
source: Human AdSCC is an uncommon but aggressive lung cancer subtype that contains a mix of clonally related adenocarcinoma and squamous cell components (Shu et al., 2013; Tochigi et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to prior literature.

claim: In murine AdSCCs, the adenocarcinoma component was continuous with, and typically circumscribed, a well-differentiated, keratinizing squamous cell carcinoma component.
source: In our mice, AdSCCs consisted of a mucinous adenocarcinoma component that was continuous with, and typically circumscribed, a well-differentiated, keratinizing squamous cell carcinoma component (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by images in Figure 4A–C.

claim: Both adenocarcinoma and squamous components of murine AdSCCs were tdTomato-positive, indicating that these tumors had arisen through Cre-mediated recombination.
source: Both components were tdTomato-positive, indicating that these tumors had arisen through Cre-mediated recombination (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by IHC images in Figure 4B.

claim: Both adenocarcinoma and squamous components of murine AdSCCs were NKX2-1-negative.
source: Although both components were NKX2-1-negative, markers of gastric differentiation were restricted to the adenocarcinoma component, and markers of squamous differentiation (including ΔNp63 and cytokeratins 5 and 14 (CK5 and CK14), but not SOX2) were selectively expressed in the SCC component (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by IHC images in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Markers of gastric differentiation were restricted to the adenocarcinoma component of murine AdSCCs.
source: Although both components were NKX2-1-negative, markers of gastric differentiation were restricted to the adenocarcinoma component, and markers of squamous differentiation (including ΔNp63 and cytokeratins 5 and 14 (CK5 and CK14), but not SOX2) were selectively expressed in the SCC component (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by IHC images in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Markers of squamous differentiation (including ΔNp63 and cytokeratins 5 and 14, but not SOX2) were selectively expressed in the SCC component of murine AdSCCs.
source: Although both components were NKX2-1-negative, markers of gastric differentiation were restricted to the adenocarcinoma component, and markers of squamous differentiation (including ΔNp63 and cytokeratins 5 and 14 (CK5 and CK14), but not SOX2) were selectively expressed in the SCC component (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by IHC images in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: In KrasLSL-G12D/+; Nkx2-1F/F; Foxa2F/F mice, FoxA2 was absent in both adenocarcinoma and squamous components, whereas FoxA1 was expressed in the adenocarcinoma components but absent in the SCC.
source: In KrasLSL-G12D/+; Nkx2-1F/F; Foxa2F/F mice, we found that FoxA2 was absent in both components, whereas FoxA1 was expressed in the adenocarcinoma components but absent in the SCC (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by IHC images in Figure 4B.

claim: AdSCC in KrasLSL-G12D/+; Nkx2-1F/F; Foxa1F/F mice exhibited FoxA1 loss in both components and FoxA2 expression only in the adenocarcinoma component.
source: AdSCC in the KrasLSL-G12D/+; Nkx2-1F/F; Foxa1F/F mouse exhibited the opposite pattern, that is, FoxA1 loss in both components and FoxA2 expression only in the adenocarcinoma component (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by IHC images in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The SCC component of murine AdSCCs is always associated with stochastic loss of FoxA1/2 expression.
source: Thus, the SCC component is always associated with stochastic loss of FoxA1/2 expression.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section, synthesizing data from Figure 4.

claim: When only one FoxA paralogue is expressed in mucinous lung adenocarcinoma, stochastic loss of the other FoxA paralogue can occur as the tumors progress.
source: These data suggest that when only one FoxA paralogue is expressed in mucinous lung adenocarcinoma, stochastic loss of the other FoxA paralogue can occur as the tumors progress.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section, synthesizing data from Figure 4.

claim: Stochastic loss of FoxA activity is associated with a profound change in differentiation state, with FoxA1/2-negative cells upregulating a keratinizing squamous differentiation program.
source: This stochastic loss of FoxA activity is associated with a profound change in differentiation state, with FoxA1/2-negative cells upregulating a keratinizing squamous differentiation program.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section, synthesizing data from Figure 4.

claim: FoxA1 and FoxA2 were expressed in the adenocarcinoma component of all human AdSCC cases analyzed.
source: FoxA1 and FoxA2 were expressed in the adenocarcinoma component of all cases.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing analysis of human AdSCC.

claim: In half of human AdSCC cases, FoxA1 and FoxA2 were both downregulated in the squamous component.
source: In half of the cases, FoxA1 and FoxA2 were both downregulated in the squamous component (n = 5 cases with complete loss of expression and n = 1 case with detectable but diminished expression).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 4D-E.

claim: All human AdSCC cases examined exhibit at least partial reduction in expression of FoxA1 or FoxA2 in the squamous component.
source: Moreover, all cases exhibit at least partial reduction in expression of FoxA1 or FoxA2 in the squamous component.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing analysis of human AdSCC.

claim: Reduced FoxA activity is commonly associated with adenosquamous transdifferentiation in human lung cancer.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that reduced FoxA activity is commonly associated with adenosquamous transdifferentiation in human lung cancer.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section, synthesizing data from Figure 4.

claim: Loss of NKX2-1, FoxA1 and FoxA2 in established neoplasia was sufficient to induce full squamous differentiation.
source: To determine whether loss of NKX2-1, FoxA1 and FoxA2 in established neoplasia was sufficient to induce full squamous differentiation, we administered tamoxifen 1 week after tumor initiation with Ad5CMV-FlpO, then analyzed tumors 4 weeks later (outline in Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the sequential recombination experiment.

claim: Almost all lesions in Nkx2-1F/F and Nkx2-1F/F; Foxa2F/F mice were ΔNp63-negative in the sequential recombination experiment.
source: Almost all lesions in Nkx2-1F/F and Nkx2-1F/F; Foxa2F/F mice were ΔNp63-negative (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by IHC images in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: All KrasFSF-G12D/+; RosaFSF-CreERT2; Nkx2-1F/F; Foxa1F/F; Foxa2F/F mice harbored numerous non-mucinous lesions lacking FoxA1/2 and HNF4α.
source: In contrast, all KrasFSF-G12D/+; RosaFSF-CreERT2; Nkx2-1F/F; Foxa1F/F; Foxa2F/F mice harbored numerous non-mucinous lesions lacking FoxA1/2 and HNF4α.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the sequential recombination experiment.

claim: Most FoxA1/2-deficient lesions in the sequential recombination experiment were morphologically similar to the SCJ-like lesions generated with Cre-mediated recombination at tumor initiation.
source: Most of these lesions were morphologically similar to the SCJ-like lesions generated with Cre-mediated recombination at tumor initiation (Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the sequential recombination experiment.

claim: Four out of eight KrasFSF-G12D/+; RosaFSF-CreERT2; Nkx2-1F/F; Foxa1F/F; Foxa2F/F mice harbored well-differentiated squamous cell carcinomas (SCCs) in the sequential recombination experiment.
source: Strikingly, four out of eight KrasFSF-G12D/+; RosaFSF-CreERT2; Nkx2-1F/F; Foxa1F/F; Foxa2F/F mice harbored well-differentiated squamous cell carcinomas (SCCs) characterized by a stratified squamous epithelium with extensive keratinization (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by images in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: SCCs in the sequential recombination model appeared to be discrete lesions and were not surrounded by HNF4α-positive mucinous adenocarcinoma.
source: In contrast to the AdSCCs that arise stochastically from mucinous adenocarcinomas (Figure 4), these SCCs appeared to be discrete lesions and were not surrounded by HNF4α-positive mucinous adenocarcinoma (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by IHC images in Figure 5B.

claim: All SCCs in the sequential recombination model expressed ΔNp63.
source: As expected, all SCCs in this model expressed ΔNp63 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by IHC images in Figure 5B.

claim: ΔNp63 was detected in a significant minority of non-keratinizing lesions in KrasFSF-G12D/+; RosaFSF-CreERT2; Nkx2-1F/F; Foxa1F/F; Foxa2F/F mice in the sequential recombination experiment.
source: Interestingly, we even detected ΔNp63 in a significant minority of non-keratinizing lesions in these mice (Figure 5B), which contrasts with the lack of ΔNp63 expression in the complete recombinants of KrasLSL-G12D/+; Nkx2-1F/F; Foxa1F/F; Foxa2F/F mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by IHC images in Figure 5B.

claim: None of the KrasLSL-G12D/+; Nkx2-1F/F; Foxa1F/F; Foxa2F/F mice infected with Ad5CMV-Cre harbored SCCs, despite the presence of multiple complete recombinants.
source: Importantly, none of the mice harbored SCCs, despite the presence of multiple complete recombinants (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Enhanced competence for squamous differentiation is likely a direct result of KRASG12D expression rather than stochastic genetic alterations accruing over time.
source: Since FoxA1/2 loss was induced only 1 week after KRASG12D expression in this experiment, it seems likely that enhanced competence for squamous differentiation is a direct result of KRASG12D expression rather than stochastic genetic alterations accruing over time.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section, based on the timing of the sequential recombination experiment.

claim: Recombination was readily detectable in the bronchioles and alveoli of Ad5-CMV-FlpO infected mice.
source: Whereas recombination was readily detectable in the bronchioles and alveoli of Ad5-CMV-FlpO infected mice, recombination was restricted to the alveoli of Ad5-SPC-FlpO infected mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by IHC images in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Recombination was restricted to the alveoli of Ad5-SPC-FlpO infected mice.
source: Whereas recombination was readily detectable in the bronchioles and alveoli of Ad5-CMV-FlpO infected mice, recombination was restricted to the alveoli of Ad5-SPC-FlpO infected mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by IHC images in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: All KrasFSF-G12D/+; RosaFSF-CreERT2; Nkx2-1F/F; Foxa1F/F; Foxa2F/F mice infected with Ad5-SPC-FlpO harbored SCJ-like lesions that were predominantly CK7-positive/CK5-negative and expressed ΔNp63 in a minority of cells.
source: All mice harbored SCJ-like lesions that were predominantly CK7-positive/CK5-negative and expressed ΔNp63 in a minority of cells.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by IHC images in Figure 6.

claim: 63% of KrasFSF-G12D/+; RosaFSF-CreERT2; Nkx2-1F/F; Foxa1F/F; Foxa2F/F mice infected with Ad5-SPC-FlpO harbored well-differentiated, keratinizing SCCs that were CK7-negative/CK5-positive and expressed ΔNp63.
source: Moreover, 63% of these mice (n = 5 out of 8) harbored well-differentiated, keratinizing SCCs that were CK7-negative/CK5-positive and expressed ΔNp63 (Figure 6, central panels and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by IHC images in Figure 6 and data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: No SCC was identified in any of the KrasLSL-G12D/+; RosaLSL-tdTomato; Nkx2-1F/F; Foxa1F/F; Foxa2F/F mice infected with Ad5-SPC-Cre.
source: Importantly, we did not identify SCC in any of the KrasLSL-G12D/+; RosaLSL-tdTomato; Nkx2-1F/F; Foxa1F/F; Foxa2F/F mice infected with Ad5-SPC-Cre.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: Loss of NKX2-1, FoxA1, and FoxA2 in SPC-positive alveolar cells has distinct outcomes depending on the state of oncogenic signaling in these cells.
source: Taken together, these data show that loss of NKX2-1, FoxA1, and FoxA2 in SPC-positive alveolar cells has distinct outcomes depending on the state of oncogenic signaling in these cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section, synthesizing data from Figure 6.

claim: When lineage specifiers are lost in normal SPC-positive cells (concomitant with KRASG12D activation), the resulting neoplasia equilibrates to a uniform SCJ-like state marked by a CK7-positive/CK5-negative immunophenotype.
source: When these lineage specifiers are lost in normal SPC-positive cells (concomitant with KRASG12D activation), the resulting neoplasia equilibrates to a uniform SCJ-like state marked by a CK7-positive/CK5-negative immunophenotype.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section, synthesizing data from Figure 6.

claim: SPC-positive cells that have already been subjected to oncogenic signaling from KRASG12D for ~1 week have the potential to undergo full squamous transdifferentiation (CK7-negative/CK5-positive) and become well-differentiated keratinizing SCCs.
source: In contrast, SPC-positive cells that have already been subjected to oncogenic signaling from KRASG12D for ~1 week have the potential to undergo full squamous transdifferentiation (CK7-negative/CK5-positive) and become well-differentiated keratinizing SCCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section, synthesizing data from Figure 6.

claim: FoxA1 and FoxA2 are required for lung adenocarcinomas to adopt a mucinous, gastric differentiation state in the absence of NKX2-1.
source: Here, we show that FoxA1 and FoxA2 are required for lung adenocarcinomas to adopt a mucinous, gastric differentiation state in the absence of NKX2-1.
evidence: This is a main conclusion stated in the Discussion section, synthesizing findings from the study.

claim: The functional redundancy of FoxA1/2 in IMA is consistent with their frequently redundant role in endodermal tissue specification.
source: Although FoxA1/2 can regulate lung adenocarcinoma biology individually in some contexts (Li et al., 2015), their functional redundancy in IMA is consistent with their frequently redundant role in endodermal tissue specification (reviewed in Golson and Kaestner, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to prior literature.

claim: FoxA1/2 likely regulate gastrointestinal differentiation programs in other types of cancer.
source: However, it appears likely that FoxA1/2 regulate gastrointestinal differentiation programs in other types of cancer.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as speculation based on findings in other cancer types.

claim: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) and its precursors often express many of the same foregut markers as NKX2-1-negative lung adenocarcinoma.
source: For example, pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) and its precursors often express many of the same foregut markers as NKX2-1-negative lung adenocarcinoma (Tata et al., 2018; Bailey et al., 2016; Prasad et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to prior literature.

claim: FoxA1/2 levels are much higher in the subset of PDAC expressing a foregut differentiation program than in those tumors with a more mesenchymal/squamous differentiation state.
source: FoxA1/2 levels are much higher in the subset of PDAC expressing a foregut differentiation program than in those tumors with a more mesenchymal/squamous differentiation state (Bailey et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to prior literature.

claim: Aberrant activation of a gastrointestinal differentiation program in prostate cancer, which can mediate castration resistance, is driven by HNF4γ in cooperation with FoxA1.
source: In addition, aberrant activation of a gastrointestinal differentiation program in prostate cancer, which can mediate castration resistance, is driven by HNF4γ in cooperation with FoxA1 (Shukla et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to prior literature.

claim: The precise consequences of FoxA1/2 loss in lung cancer are highly dependent on the specific context in which it occurs.
source: Interestingly, the precise consequences of FoxA1/2 loss in lung cancer are highly dependent on the specific context in which it occurs (model, Figure 7).
evidence: This is a main conclusion stated in the Discussion section, synthesizing findings from the study and illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: In the absence of FoxA1/2 activity, Nkx2-1 deletion causes normal lung epithelial cells to adopt a cell fate resembling the transitional epithelium that localizes immediately proximal to the glandular stomach.
source: Thus, in the absence of FoxA1/2 activity, Nkx2-1 deletion causes normal lung epithelial cells to adopt a cell fate resembling the transitional epithelium that localizes immediately proximal to the glandular stomach.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Discussion section, synthesizing findings from Figure 3.

claim: Signaling from KRASG12D enhances the capacity of SPC-positive cells to activate a squamous differentiation program in the absence of NKX2-1 and FoxA1/2.
source: In contrast, both stochastic (Figure 4) and engineered (Figures 5–6) loss of FoxA1/2 in established KRASG12D-driven lesions initiated in SPC-positive cells was accompanied by activation of a robust squamous differentiation program, as evidenced by a stratified multi-layered epithelium with extensive keratinization and expression of ΔNp63 and CK5. These data suggest that signaling from KRASG12D enhances the capacity of SPC-positive cells to activate a squamous differentiation program in the absence of NKX2-1 and FoxA1/2.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Discussion section, synthesizing findings from Figures 4-6.

claim: ΔNp63 is an activator of squamous differentiation and is generally thought to function as an oncogene in SCC.
source: ΔNp63 is an activator of squamous differentiation and is generally thought to function as an oncogene in SCC (Watanabe et al., 2014), so the increased levels of ΔNp63 when Nkx2-1;Foxa1/2 deletion occurs in established lesions (Figures 5–6) vs. at tumor initiation (Figure 3) are likely to be one major factor that dictates whether cells adopt an SCJ-like vs. SCC fate.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to prior literature.

claim: The increased levels of ΔNp63 when Nkx2-1;Foxa1/2 deletion occurs in established lesions vs. at tumor initiation are likely to be one major factor that dictates whether cells adopt an SCJ-like vs. SCC fate.
source: ΔNp63 is an activator of squamous differentiation and is generally thought to function as an oncogene in SCC (Watanabe et al., 2014), so the increased levels of ΔNp63 when Nkx2-1;Foxa1/2 deletion occurs in established lesions (Figures 5–6) vs. at tumor initiation (Figure 3) are likely to be one major factor that dictates whether cells adopt an SCJ-like vs. SCC fate.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as speculation based on the data.

claim: In KrasG12D; Lkb1 conditional mice, CC10-positive lung epithelial cells are the predominant cell of origin for adenosquamous carcinomas, whereas SPC-positive cells mainly give rise to adenocarcinomas.
source: In KrasG12D; Lkb1 conditional mice CC10-positive lung epithelial cells are the predominant cell of origin for adenosquamous carcinomas, whereas SPC-positive cells mainly give rise to adenocarcinomas (Nagaraj et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to prior literature.

claim: In murine models driven by SOX2 expression and either deletion of Pten and Cdkn2ab or Nkx2-1, both CC10-positive and SPC-positive cell types can give rise to SCCs, although CC10-positive cells appeared to do so more efficiently.
source: In other murine models driven by SOX2 expression and either deletion of Pten and Cdkn2ab (Ferone et al., 2016) or Nkx2-1 (7), both cell types can give rise to SCCs, although CC10-positive cells appeared to do so more efficiently.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to prior literature.

claim: Context is critical for the effect of FoxA1/2 loss on tumor growth.
source: Context also appears to be critical for the effect of FoxA1/2 loss on tumor growth.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a conclusion from the study.

claim: Nkx2-1 deletion augments KRASG12D-driven tumorigenesis.
source: We have previously shown that Nkx2-1 deletion augments KRASG12D-driven tumorigenesis (Snyder et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to prior work.

claim: Concomitant Foxa1/2 deletion at initiation reverses the tumor-promoting effect of Nkx2-1 deletion.
source: Concomitant Foxa1/2 deletion at initiation reverses this phenotype (Figure 2), showing that when FoxA1/2 are absent at tumor initiation, NKX2-1-negative lesions equilibrate to a low proliferation state that never progresses to macroscopic disease.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: The stochastic emergence of macroscopic FoxA1/2-negative AdSCCs argues that there is a selective advantage to loss of FoxA1/2 in some established lung neoplasia.
source: However, the stochastic emergence of macroscopic FoxA1/2-negative AdSCCs (Figure 4) argues that there is a selective advantage to loss of FoxA1/2 in some established lung neoplasia.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: 43% of human lung SCC cases lacked FoxA1 expression by IHC, and FoxA1 positivity was significantly correlated with unfavorable survival.
source: For example, one study of human lung SCC reported that 43% of cases lacked FoxA1 expression by IHC, and that FoxA1 positivity was significantly correlated with unfavorable survival (Deutsch et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to prior literature.

claim: In PDAC, FoxA1 can promote metastasis.
source: In PDAC, FoxA1 can promote metastasis (Roe et al., 2017), despite the fact low levels of FoxA1/2 (as well as other lineage specifiers associated with endodermal differentiation) are found in the subtype of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma that confers the worst prognosis (Bailey et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to prior literature.

claim: Low levels of FoxA1/2 are found in the subtype of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma that confers the worst prognosis.
source: In PDAC, FoxA1 can promote metastasis (Roe et al., 2017), despite the fact low levels of FoxA1/2 (as well as other lineage specifiers associated with endodermal differentiation) are found in the subtype of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma that confers the worst prognosis (Bailey et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to prior literature.

claim: FoxA1 and FoxA2 regulate the growth and gastric identity of NKX2-1-negative lung adenocarcinoma.
source: In summary, this work expands our understanding of the lineage specifiers that coordinately regulate the growth and identity of lung adenocarcinoma. We show that FoxA1 and FoxA2 regulate the growth and gastric identity of NKX2-1-negative lung adenocarcinoma.
evidence: This is a main conclusion stated in the Discussion section, synthesizing findings from the study.

claim: In the absence of FoxA1/2 activity, NKX2-1-negative tumor cells adopt a more proximal cell fate with features of either the transitional epithelium of the SCJ or the squamous epithelium of the forestomach/esophagus, depending on the context of FoxA1/2 loss.
source: In the absence of FoxA1/2 activity, NKX2-1-negative tumor cells adopt a more proximal cell fate with features of either the transitional epithelium of the SCJ or the squamous epithelium of the forestomach/esophagus, depending on the context of FoxA1/2 loss.
evidence: This is a main conclusion stated in the Discussion section, synthesizing findings from the study.

claim: Squamous transdifferentiation has been linked to drug resistance in human lung adenocarcinomas.
source: Squamous transdifferentiation has been linked to drug resistance in human lung adenocarcinomas (Hou et al., 2017), and it will be interesting to determine whether FoxA1/2 downregulation plays a role in this process.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to prior literature.

claim: The effects of lineage specifier inactivation in cancer can be highly context-dependent.
source: More broadly, our results show that the effects of lineage specifier inactivation in cancer can be highly context-dependent, and provide an experimental system for future work to elucidate the mechanistic basis for this specificity.
evidence: This is a main conclusion stated in the Discussion section, synthesizing findings from the study.
